Markov chain

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Probability and statistics Probability theory Markov process
OurBigBook.com Words: 19k Articles: 355
The term Markov chain commonly denotes a Markov process on a finite or countable state space. Time may be discrete, as for a daily record, or continuous, as for a continuous-time Markov chain. Some authors also use “Markov chain” for discrete-time processes on more general state spaces; specifying both time and state space avoids this ambiguity.
For a Discrete-time Markov chain, its initial probability distribution μ0​ and transition matrix P specify the probability of each finite path:
P(X0​=i0​,…,Xn​=in​)=μ0​(i0​)∏k=0n−1​Pik​ik+1​​.
(1)
This is the Markov factorization, obtained by applying conditional probability repeatedly. See Hao Wu's MIT lecture 1, definition and distribution evolution.
For the constructed sunny/rainy Markov chain below, starting sunny makes the path sunny, rainy, sunny have probability 1×0.2×0.4=0.08. Starting instead with stationary distribution (2/3,1/3) makes that path's probability (2/3)×0.2×0.4=4/75. The transition probabilities are identical in both experiments; the initial probability distribution distinguishes them.

Acyclic Markov chain

Words: 32
Markov chain OurBigBook.com
An acyclic Markov chain has no directed cycle among its nonabsorbing states. Its finite transition dependencies can therefore be evaluated in reverse topological order instead of solving a general system of equations.

Absorbing Markov chain

Words: 37
Markov chain OurBigBook.com
A Markov chain with at least one absorbing state, such that from each state an absorbing state can be reached. In a finite such chain, absorption occurs with probability 1. Expected times to absorption satisfy a linear system obtained by conditioning on the first transition.

Harmonic function for a Markov chain (Ph=h)

Words: 759 Articles: 1
Markov chain OurBigBook.com
A harmonic function assigns a value to each state of a Markov chain such that one transition leaves its expected value unchanged. This turns a question about many possible future sample paths, such as which endpoint is reached first, into a local averaging rule. For a transition matrix P, a real-valued function h is harmonic at state i when
h(i)=(Ph)(i)=∑j​Pij​h(j)=Ei​[h(X1​)].
(2)
Here Ei​ means expected value conditional on starting at X0​=i; on a countable state space the sum must be absolutely convergent. If this holds at every state, write Ph=h. At an absorbing state the equation is automatic, so prescribed boundary conditions supply information that the averaging rule cannot.
For a finite Markov chain, choose a boundary set B that can be reached from every state, and assign boundary values b. If TB​ is its first hitting time, the harmonic extension is
h(i)=Ei​[b(XTB​​)],h∣B​=b.
(3)
Choosing b to be the indicator function of one target within B gives a hitting probability. This is a discrete Dirichlet problem: enforce the averaging rule outside B and fix the values on B. See Hao Wu's MIT lecture 8, harmonic extension, slide 5. The construction extends the mean-value idea of a harmonic function; for a random walk on a graph it is a discrete harmonic function.

Five-state harmonic absorption example (hi​=i/4,ti​=i(4−i))

Words: 572
Harmonic function for a Markov chain OurBigBook.com
Take a birth-death chain on {0,1,2,3,4}. At each interior state, move up one state with probability p=1/2 and down one state with probability q=1/2. The endpoints are absorbing states: P00​=P44​=1. This is a small gambler's ruin model in which the state can represent capital, and reaching 4 is success.
Let Ta​=inf{n≥0:Xn​=a} be the hitting time of endpoint a, and let T=min(T0​,T4​) be the first endpoint hitting time. The desired hitting probability is hi​=Pi​(T4​<T0​). First-step analysis and the Markov property give
h0​=0,h4​=1,hi​=21​hi−1​+21​hi+1​(i=1,2,3).
(4)
The interior equation says adjacent differences are equal. Four equal increments must bridge the boundary values 0 and 1, so
hi​=4i​,(h0​,h1​,h2​,h3​,h4​)=(0,41​,21​,43​,1).
(5)
For example, from state 2 the hitting probability is 1/2, and its one-step average is 21​(1/4)+21​(3/4)=1/2. Individual sample paths can wander back and forth, but the same averaging rule already accounts for all of them.
Now ask how long it takes to reach either endpoint. The expected hitting time ti​=Ei​T counts steps, including the transition that first reaches an endpoint. First-step analysis gives
t0​=t4​=0,ti​=1+21​ti−1​+21​ti+1​(i=1,2,3).
(6)
This is a discrete Poisson equation, (I−P)t=1 in the interior. The extra 1 counts the step just taken. The quadratic values
ti​=i(4−i),(t0​,t1​,t2​,t3​,t4​)=(0,3,4,3,0)
(7)
satisfy the equations; from state 2, t2​=1+21​(3)+21​(3)=4 steps. The hitting probability is harmonic, whereas the expected hitting time has a nonzero source term. These are special cases of expected duration of symmetric gambler's ruin; see Hao Wu's MIT lecture 16, gambler's ruin, slide 9.
For a biased random walk with p=0.6 upward and q=0.4 downward, keep the same absorbing states. The interior harmonic equation becomes hi​=phi+1​+qhi−1​. Using biased gambler's ruin probability with these boundary values gives
r=pq​=32​,hi​=1−r41−ri​,(h0​,h1​,h2​,h3​,h4​)=(0,6527​,139​,6557​,1).
(8)
The three interior hitting probabilities are approximately 0.415385, 0.692308, and 0.876923. Thus starting at 2 now succeeds about 69.23% of the time. A direct check is 0.6(57/65)+0.4(27/65)=9/13. The curved profile reflects the unequal transition weights: its successive increments shrink by the factor q/p=2/3. The formula, with the endpoint denoted T there, is verified in Karger and Lynch's MIT lecture 26, sections 2.3-2.4; the five-state numbers here are direct substitutions.
Why does harmonic averaging produce the correct hitting probability? With the natural filtration Fn​=σ(X0​,…,Xn​), the Markov property gives the conditional expectation identity
E[h(Xn+1​)∣Fn​]=(Ph)(Xn​).
(9)
For a function harmonic everywhere, this makes h(Xn​) a martingale whenever it is integrable. For a function harmonic only in the interior, Mn​=h(Xn∧T​) is a stopped martingale. In either five-state example, 0≤Mn​≤1. Also, from any interior state at most three consecutive upward steps reach 4, with probability at least p3>0. Repeated three-step blocks give Pi​(T>3k)≤(1−p3)k, so T is almost surely finite and has finite expected value; compare finite-interval exit times have geometric tails. Applying optional stopping at n∧T and then the bounded convergence theorem gives
hi​=Ei​[h(XT​)]=Pi​(XT​=4).
(10)
The boundedness and finite hitting time justify this passage to the limit. See Steven Lalley's notes, harmonic functions and stopped expectations, theorem 1, and stopped martingale in discrete time for this bounded version of optional stopping.
Uniqueness has a short maximum principle explanation. On a finite state space, the difference of two harmonic extensions with the same boundary conditions is zero on the boundary. If its positive maximum occurs inside, the weighted average forces every successor with positive transition probability to have the same maximum. A path to the boundary propagates that maximum to zero, a contradiction. Applying the argument to the negative of the difference proves uniqueness. Reachability of the boundary is essential: an interior closed communicating class can retain an arbitrary constant.

Two-lane Markov chain with a deterministic restart (qc​=(5​−1)/2)

Words: 138
Markov chain OurBigBook.com
Take states 0,n,n′ for n≥1, with 0→1′ deterministic and transitions n→n−1 with probability q, n→(n+1)′ with probability p=1−q, n′→n with probability q, and n′→(n+1)′ with probability p. The Markov chain is transient for q<qc​, null recurrent for q=qc​, and positive recurrent for q>qc​. To see the Markov chain recurrence threshold, eliminate the primed-state hitting probabilities to obtain p(1+q)an+1​−(1+pq)an​+qan−1​=0, with characteristic roots 1 and q/(1−q2). Boundedness forces return with probability one when the second root is at least one. When it is below one, the minimal nonnegative solution gives return probability q2/p<1 from 0. In the positive recurrent case, put t=(1−q2)/q and D=q2+q−1. The stationary distribution is π0​=D/[q(q+2)], πn​=(π0​/q)tn−1 and πn′​=π0​tn−1. It follows from balance across each level cut and sums to one; at criticality the invariant weights cannot be normalized.

This Markov chain on the symmetric group holds with probability 1/n and assigns probability 2/n2 to each unordered transposition. Its stationary distribution is uniform, and its ordinary spectral gap is 2/n for n≥2. The latter follows from the Aldous spectral gap theorem: the single-label continuous-time Markov chain has rate 2/n2 between every pair of positions, whose mean-zero eigenvalues are all −2/n.

Markov chain OurBigBook.com
For a finite, time-homogeneous Discrete-time Markov chain with row-stochastic transition matrix P, a state a is absorbing exactly when Paa​=1. Nonnegativity and the row sum then force Paj​=0 for j=a: once entered, a is never left. Equivalently, {a} is a closed communicating class. A larger closed communicating class may keep moving internally; closure means confinement to a set, whereas absorption at a state means remaining at one point.
An absorbing state is useful for recording a terminal outcome: after a toy routine finishes, keep its outcome in the state space so that the same transition matrix still describes subsequent steps. Calling a finite Markov chain absorbing usually also requires that some absorbing state be accessible from every state. Merely containing an absorbing state is insufficient: another closed communicating class could prevent absorption. See Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability, section 11.2 for this convention.

P=​1/21/400​1/41/400​1/4010​01/201​​.

tu​=1+21​tu​+41​tv​,tv​=1+41​tu​+41​tv​.

Starting at u therefore ends at A with probability 0.6 and takes 3.2 steps on average to reach either terminal state. The terminal hitting time counts the transition into the outcome, but no later self-transitions. Markov chain OurBigBook.com
For a finite, time-homogeneous Discrete-time Markov chain with row-stochastic transition matrix P, irreducibility means
∀i,j∈S∃n≥0:(Pn)ij​>0.
(30)
Equivalently, all states form one communicating class. The step count may depend on i,j; irreducibility does not require every one-step transition probability to be positive. Drawing an arrow i→j whenever Pij​>0 makes the condition exactly that of a strongly connected directed graph. It is a property of the entire chosen state space, independent of the initial probability distribution.
Irreducibility describes where the Markov chain can travel; aperiodicity describes the possible lengths of return paths. For example, restricting the second diagram in communicating class to its closed pair {c1​,c2​} gives
C=(01​10​),C2k=I,C2k+1=C(k≥0),
(31)
where I is the identity matrix. This Markov chain is irreducible, but each state's period of a state in a Markov chain is two. Every destination is reachable, yet a given destination cannot be reached at every sufficiently large step count. Starting at c1​ produces alternating one-time probability distributions. See Hao Wu's MIT lecture 2, irreducibility and periods for the definitions.
Adding a holding probability of a Markov chain ε at each state, with 0<ε<1, gives
Cε​=εI+(1−ε)C.
(32)
The arrows between the two states remain, so the Markov chain remains irreducible. A positive one-step return makes it an aperiodic Markov chain. At ε=1/2, both rows are (1/2,1/2) and C1/2n​=C1/2​ for every n≥1: the initial state is forgotten after one step. At ε=1, however, both states become absorbing states, giving two separate communicating classes and losing irreducibility.
For a finite Markov chain, irreducibility guarantees a unique stationary distribution with positive weight at every state. Adding aperiodicity guarantees convergence μ0​Pn→π for every initial probability distribution; see Hao Wu's MIT lecture 4, convergence theorem. The Markov chain ergodic theorem gives convergence of empirical visit frequencies even for an irreducible periodic Markov chain. These results explain why checking connectivity is a useful first step before studying equilibrium. Conversely, any absorbing state prevents irreducibility if there is another state: it cannot reach that state. The one-state Markov chain is the exception.

Here the graph has 2n vertices and m≥1 edges. The bound is a deliberately loose canonical paths Poincare bound, sufficient for polynomial mixing time when both activity and reciprocal activity are polynomially bounded. Order the alternating graph paths and cycles of I△F canonically. Convert each component from initial matching in a graph I to final matching in a graph F by moving an unmatched endpoint using exchanges; open a cycle with one deletion and finish it with one addition.
At an intermediate matching in a graph M, the complementary encoding K=I△F△M is a matching in a graph away from the active component and has at most two degree-two vertices. Remove at most two edges to obtain a matching in a graph K′. Record those edges and one bit selecting the initial alternating colour on the active component. For a fixed directed transition this data reconstructs K, I△F, the active component and its ordering, and then I,F; common edges are M∩K. There are at most 2(m+1)2 auxiliary records per K′.
If d=∣K∣−∣K′∣≤2, then πλ​(I)πλ​(F)=λdπλ​(M)πλ​(K′). The transition capacity is at least πλ​(M)/(2mmax(λ,λ−1)), and the path length is at most 4n. Summing over the injective encodings proves the displayed path congestion bound.

For the non-backtracking random walk, directed-edge types outer-outer, outer-inner, inner-outer and inner-inner give remaining means 13/2,9/2,15/2,21/4. Parity balance on entry to a period-two Markov class

Words: 100
Periodic Markov chain OurBigBook.com
Suppose a Markov chain leaves transient states and enters a closed two-state class which alternates deterministically. If entry is always into the first state, let a and b be the probabilities of entering at even and odd times. After the probability of still being transient tends to zero, the even-time probabilities at the two recurrent states tend to a,b, while the odd-time probabilities tend to b,a. Individual limits therefore exist exactly when a=b. A periodic recurrent class can thus have convergent state probabilities from particular transient starting states even though convergence fails from its own states.

Countable-state Markov chain convergence theorem (Pn(i,j)→πj​)

Words: 83
Convergence to an invariant distribution OurBigBook.com
For an irreducible Markov chain on a finite or countable state space, a positive recurrent state implies a unique stationary distribution π. If the chain is also an aperiodic Markov chain, its transition probabilities satisfy the displayed limit for every pair of states. The same limit holds from any initial probability distribution by bounded convergence. Positive recurrence cannot be omitted in the countably infinite case, and aperiodicity is required for ordinary, rather than averaged, convergence. This is the standard discrete-time convergence theorem; the finite-state statement alone does not cover unbounded renewal countdowns.

An irreducible chain shares these properties among all its states.

Markov chain ergodic theorem

Words: 79
Finite Markov chain OurBigBook.com
For an irreducible finite Markov chain with stationary distribution π, the fraction of visits to any state j converges almost surely to πj​, for every initial state. More generally, the empirical average of a function of the state converges to its average under π. Aperiodicity is needed for convergence of the one-time distributions, but not for this empirical-frequency conclusion. Regeneration at returns to a state proves the conclusion by applying the strong law to independent excursion lengths and excursion rewards.

Finite Markov chain OurBigBook.com
For a real function f on a finite state space, a state minimizing f satisfies Pf≥f, so strictly negative drift cannot hold at every state. Equivalently, telescoping the expected value would give Ex​f(Xn​)=f(x)−nδ, contradicting boundedness of f. Constant negative drift is useful before a target is reached; it must be restricted to the states outside that target.

Communicating class

Words: 783 Articles: 8
Markov chain OurBigBook.com
In a finite, time-homogeneous Discrete-time Markov chain with row-stochastic transition matrix P, write i→j when j is accessible from i, meaning (Pn)ij​>0 for some n≥0. States communicate, written i↔j, when both i→j and j→i. Communication is an equivalence relation, and a communicating class is an entire equivalence class
C(i)={j∈S:i↔j}.
(65)
Thus communicating classes form a partition of the state space; a smaller mutually communicating subset is not itself a class. See Maria Cameron's Markov Chains notes, section 1.2.
The allowance of zero steps matters: P0=I, the identity matrix, makes i→i true even for a state with no possible positive-time return. Symmetry is built into communication. For transitivity, concatenate a positive-probability path from i to j with one from j to k, and do the same in reverse. These observations prove the equivalence relation directly. One-way accessibility alone is not symmetric and does not define the classes; see Accessible state of a Markov chain.
A closed communicating class satisfies Pij​=0 for every i∈C and j∈/C. Once entered, it cannot be left. A singleton class is an absorbing state exactly when it is closed. An open communicating class has an outgoing transition; after a path leaves it, it cannot return, since that would make the visited outside states communicate with it. The internal motion of a closed class can nevertheless continue forever.
For this constructed example, in state order (s,c1​,c2​,a), the transition matrix is
P=​1/2000​1/4010​0100​1/4001​​.
(66)
There are exactly three communicating classes: {s}, {c1​,c2​}, and {a}. Only the first is open. The second is closed but neither of its states is an absorbing state; they alternate deterministically. Although s→c2​ via c1​, the reverse accessibility fails. A direct matrix power check gives (P2)s,c2​​=1/4 and (P2)c2​,s​=0.
Starting at s, let τ be the first hitting time of either closed class. Staying at s for n steps has probability 2−n, so Ps​(τ>n)=2−n and Es​τ=∑n≥0​2−n=2. The two eventual destination classes each have probability ∑k≥0​(1/2)k(1/4)=1/2. Hence the hitting probability of the absorbing state a is only 1/2, and its unconditional expected hitting time from s is infinite: on half the paths it is never hit. In particular, entering a closed class with certainty does not imply entering an absorbing state with certainty.
Classifying the state space separates two questions: which closed region will eventually be entered, and how does the Markov chain move inside that region? In this example the restriction to {c1​,c2​} is an irreducible Markov chain with period two; the restriction to {a} is a one-state irreducible Markov chain with period one. The whole Markov chain is reducible. The absorbing state example illustrates a different possibility: every closed class is a singleton, so eventual class selection is also terminal outcome selection.

Equivalently, (Pn)ij​>0 for some n≥0, allowing a zero-step path when i=j. Accessibility is reflexive and transitive; communicating states require accessibility in both directions. See Ward Whitt's lecture notes of September 24, 2013, classification of states. In the closed-cycle example in communicating class, s→c2​ despite Ps,c2​​=0, because Ps,c1​​Pc1​,c2​​=1/4>0; c2​→s fails at every step count.

Open communicating class

Words: 60
Communicating class OurBigBook.com
A communicating class of a Markov chain is open when a state in the class has positive probability of transitioning to a state outside it. Once a path leaves, it cannot return to the class: a return path would make the outside state communicate with the class. Every open class consists of transient states. Conversely, a finite transient communicating class is open; an infinite closed communicating class can be transient.

Stationary distribution (πP=π)

Words: 346 Articles: 1
Markov chain OurBigBook.com
A stationary distribution is a probability distribution π preserved by a Markov chain's evolution. For a Discrete-time Markov chain in the row convention,
πP=π,πi​≥0,∑i​πi​=1.
(68)
Thus π is a normalized nonnegative left eigenvector of the transition matrix for eigenvalue one. Starting with X0​ distributed as π makes every Xn​ have that same probability distribution. For a time-homogeneous Markov chain, the path probabilities are also unchanged by shifting all observation times together: the process has strict stationarity. This does not mean its individual paths are constant. See Hao Wu's MIT lecture 2, stationary distributions.
For the sunny/rainy transition matrix, write π=(a,1−a). The sunny component of πP=π gives a=0.8a+0.4(1−a), so 0.6a=0.4 and
π=(32​,31​),πP=(158​+152​,152​+153​)=π.
(69)
Moreover,
πS​PSR​=32​51​=152​=31​52​=πR​PRS​.
(70)
These equal stationary flows verify detailed balance and show that the Markov chain is reversible. The diagonal detailed balance equations hold automatically. Only 1/3 of the stationary days are rainy, but 0.6 of the days following a rainy day are rainy: stationarity permits dependence.
A finite Markov chain that is an irreducible Markov chain has a unique stationary distribution. If it is also an aperiodic Markov chain, μ0​Pn→π for every initial probability distribution. The sunny/rainy example satisfies both conditions: both directions are possible and each state has a positive holding probability of a Markov chain. See Hao Wu's MIT lecture 4, convergence theorem. For an infinite state space, the additional positive recurrence hypothesis in the countable-state Markov chain convergence theorem matters.
Existence of a stationary distribution alone does not give this convergence. Consider the deterministic two-cycle
C=(01​10​),π=(21​,21​).

Here πC=π, but starting in the first state gives alternating probability distributions (1,0),(0,1),(1,0),…. Its period of a state in a Markov chain is two. The running fraction of visits to either state nevertheless tends to 1/2, illustrating the Markov chain ergodic theorem. Starting with π instead keeps the one-time probability distributions stationary even though every path alternates.
